passages.title: Joshua receives the charge
passages.summary: After Moses dies, the LORD tells Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan. He promises to give them every place their feet tread. He says he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses. He tells Joshua three times to be strong and courageous. Joshua must keep the law and think on it day and night. Joshua tells the officers to prepare to cross in three days. He reminds Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh to fight beside their brothers. They promise to obey him as they obeyed Moses.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The Church lesson connects courage with God’s presence and repeated scripture study. What is Joshua told to do with the book of the law (verse 8)?

contextNote.title: Leadership remains under the law
contextNote.text: Joshua is a new commander facing a war. The LORD’s orders in verses 6–9 say almost nothing about tactics. Three times he says to be strong and courageous. In between, verse 8 gives one practice: keep the law in his mouth always. Success is tied to doing “all that is written in it.” This matches the rule for kings in Deuteronomy 17:18–19. Israel’s leader does not stand above the law he enforces.

passages.title: Rahab protects the spies
passages.summary: Joshua secretly sends two spies to Jericho. They stay in the house of Rahab, a prostitute. The king sends for them, and Rahab hides them under flax on her roof. She tells the king’s men that the spies already left. She tells the spies the LORD has given Israel the land. She asks them to spare her family, and they swear to it. She lets them down by a cord from her window in the city wall. She must tie a scarlet cord there and keep her family inside.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Rahab as an example of faith expressed through action. What does Rahab say about the LORD in verse 11?

contextNote.title: The first witness comes from outside
contextNote.text: The spies were sent to learn about Jericho. What they learn comes from Rahab’s mouth. She retells the Red Sea and the defeat of two kings (verses 9–10). Verse 11 calls the LORD “God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.” Moses used nearly the same words in Deuteronomy 4:39. So the first clear statement of faith in the land comes from a Canaanite woman. She then acts on it at risk to herself (verses 4–6 and 15).

passages.title: Crossing the Jordan
passages.summary: Israel camps at the Jordan for three days. The officers tell the people to follow the ark at a distance. Joshua tells them to make themselves ready for the LORD’s wonders. The LORD says he will make Joshua great, as he was with Moses. The priests carry the ark to the river, which is in flood at harvest. When their feet touch the water, the river stops and piles up far upstream. The priests stand on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crosses over near Jericho.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The Church lesson connects the crossing with trust in Christ and the promise of baptism. When does the water stop, according to verses 13 and 15?

contextNote.title: The crossing gives the priests a public task
contextNote.text: Verse 15 notes that the Jordan was in flood at harvest time. The river does not part while the people watch from the bank. Verse 13 ties the stopping to the priests’ feet resting in the water. They must step in while it is still running. Verse 17 has them stand in the riverbed until the whole nation is across. The priests go first and leave last. Verse 7 says the event also shows that God is with Joshua.

passages.title: Stones for remembrance
passages.summary: After the crossing, the LORD tells Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Each carries a stone from the riverbed where the priests stood. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan. About forty thousand armed men cross toward Jericho. That day the people honor Joshua as they had honored Moses. When the priests come out, the river returns and overflows its banks. Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there. The stones are for children who will ask what they mean.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to recognize God’s help and teach the next generation. What question will children ask about the stones (verse 6)?

contextNote.title: A memorial requires an explanation
contextNote.text: A pile of stones says nothing without someone to speak for it. Verse 6 expects children to ask what the stones mean. Verse 7 gives parents the answer to pass on. The stones come from the exact place the priests stood (verse 3). So they are evidence as well as a marker. Verses 21–24 repeat the question and link the Jordan to the Red Sea. The aim reaches past Israel: that all peoples may know the LORD’s hand.

passages.title: Passover and the commander
passages.summary: The kings of the land hear about the Jordan and lose heart. The LORD tells Joshua to circumcise the men born in the wilderness. The older generation had died there for not listening. The LORD says he has rolled away Egypt’s reproach, and the place is named Gilgal. Israel keeps the Passover in the plains of Jericho. They eat the produce of the land, and the manna stops. Near Jericho Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword. He is commander of the LORD’s army, and Joshua bows and removes his sandals.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The older manual proposes that the commander may be the Lord. It acknowledges the limited details. Joshua asks whose side the man is on (verse 13). How does the man answer in verse 14?

contextNote.title: The commander changes Joshua's question
contextNote.text: Joshua’s question in verse 13 offers two choices: for us or for our enemies. The man’s first word is “No.” He is not a soldier for either side to claim. He commands the LORD’s army, and Joshua is the one who must take a side. Joshua understands at once and falls on his face. He then asks the better question: what does his lord say? Verse 15 repeats what Moses heard at the bush (Exodus 3:5).

passages.title: Jericho and Rahab’s rescue
passages.summary: Jericho is shut tight. The LORD tells Joshua to march around it once a day for six days. Seven priests carry ram’s horn trumpets before the ark. On day seven they circle seven times and shout, and the wall falls flat. Israel destroys everyone in the city, young and old, and the animals. The two spies bring out Rahab and her whole family. The city is burned, and its metals go to the LORD’s treasury. Rahab lives in Israel from then on, and Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds Jericho.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies trust and obedience through the account of Jericho. Why was Rahab saved, according to verse 25?

contextNote.title: Destruction and rescue occupy the same account
contextNote.text: The chapter gives Jericho’s fall in verse 20 and its destruction in verse 21. Verse 21 lists who died: men, women, young, and old. Verses 22–25 then tell of one house that was spared. The spies keep the oath of 2:14 and bring out Rahab’s whole family. Verse 25 gives the reason: “she hid the messengers.” A Canaanite woman now lives “in the middle of Israel.” The account sets rescue beside destruction and does not explain away either.

passages.title: Achan and defeat at Ai
passages.summary: Achan of Judah secretly takes some of the goods devoted to the LORD. Israel sends about three thousand men against Ai, and they are driven back. Thirty-six die, and the people lose heart. Joshua falls before the ark and asks why God brought them over the Jordan. The LORD says Israel has sinned and stolen devoted things. The next morning Judah is singled out, then a family, then Achan. Achan confesses that he hid a robe, silver, and gold under his tent. Israel stones him and his household in the valley of Achor.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies how Achan’s hidden choice harms other people. What steps does his confession name in verse 21?

contextNote.title: Hidden goods create a public crisis
contextNote.text: Verse 1 blames “the children of Israel” for what one man did. Thirty-six soldiers die before anyone knows why (verse 5). Achan’s confession in verse 21 walks through the steps: saw, coveted, took. Then he hid the goods in the ground under his tent. What was buried in private had already cost lives in public. Verse 11 says the theft also involved deceit. The penalty falls on his household too, with no comment given (verses 24–25).

passages.title: Ai and the law at Ebal
passages.summary: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and to set an ambush behind Ai. Joshua hides men west of the city and camps the rest to the north. Israel pretends to flee, and every man of Ai chases them. Joshua stretches out his javelin, and the hidden men take and burn the city. Twelve thousand people of Ai die, and its king is hanged. Israel keeps the livestock and goods this time. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and writes the law on stones. He reads every word to all Israel, with the women, children, and foreigners.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The manual connects the public reading with Moses’s instructions. Who is named among the hearers in verse 35?

contextNote.title: The law is heard beyond the fighting force
contextNote.text: After two battles Joshua stops the war for a reading. Moses ordered this at Mount Ebal in Deuteronomy 27:2–8. Joshua builds the altar, writes the law on stones, and reads it all. Verse 34 says he read “the blessing and the curse.” Verse 35 names those who heard: women, little ones, and foreigners. None of these fought at Ai. The law belongs to the whole people, not only to its army.

passages.title: The Gibeonite agreement
passages.summary: The kings west of the Jordan join to fight Israel. The people of Gibeon choose a trick. They come with worn sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread, and claim a far country. Israel’s men taste their food and do not ask the LORD. Joshua makes a covenant to let them live, and the leaders swear to it. Three days later Israel learns that they live nearby. The people grumble, but the leaders will not break an oath sworn by the LORD. The Gibeonites become woodcutters and water carriers for the altar.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The older Church manual studies keeping a promise when its cost becomes clear. What did Israel’s men fail to do in verse 14?

contextNote.title: An oath survives a failed decision
contextNote.text: Verse 14 names Israel’s mistake: they tested the bread and did not ask the LORD. The covenant in verse 15 rests on a lie the Gibeonites told. Three days later the truth comes out. The leaders still say, “We have sworn to them by the LORD” (verse 19). An oath in God’s name binds them even though they were tricked. So the Gibeonites live, as servants at the altar (verse 27). Their reason in verse 24 is the same fear Rahab named in 2:9–11.

passages.title: The southern coalition
passages.summary: Five Amorite kings, led by Jerusalem’s king, attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Gibeon begs Joshua not to abandon it. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and surprises them. The LORD throws them into confusion and sends great hailstones. Joshua asks for the sun and moon to stand still, and they do. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are later put to death. Joshua takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. He holds the southern land because the LORD fought for Israel.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The older Church manual compares the long day with Helaman 12. Gibeon asks Joshua not to abandon it (verse 6). How does Joshua respond in verses 7–9?

contextNote.title: An agreement creates a duty in war
contextNote.text: Gibeon won its treaty by a trick in chapter 9. Now the treaty brings an attack, and Gibeon calls for help (verse 6). Joshua could have let the kings remove a problem for him. He marches all night to keep the oath (verse 9). The LORD backs that choice with hail and a long day (verses 11–14). So this battle is fought for an ally Israel did not want. Second Samuel 21:1–2 later treats breaking this oath as a serious wrong.

passages.title: Hazor and northern war
passages.summary: Jabin king of Hazor gathers the northern kings with horses and chariots. Their army is like the sand of the seashore. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear. Joshua attacks suddenly at the waters of Merom and wins. He cripples their horses and burns their chariots, as the LORD said. He burns Hazor, the leading city, but not the other cities on their mounds. The war with these kings lasts a long time. Joshua takes the whole land, and the land rests from war.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: How does Joshua respond to God’s instructions before the battle (verses 6 and 9)? What does verse 18 say about how long the war took?

contextNote.title: The account preserves a long campaign
contextNote.text: Chapters 10 and 11 can read like a quick sweep through the land. Verse 18 corrects that: “Joshua made war a long time.” Caleb’s words in 14:10 suggest several years had passed. Verse 13 adds that most cities were left standing, and only Hazor was burned. Verse 22 notes that some Anakim remained in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. So the summary “the whole land” in verse 23 has stated limits. Chapter 13:1 says much land still remained.

passages.title: The defeated kings listed
passages.summary: This chapter lists the kings Israel defeated. East of the Jordan, Moses defeated Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan. Their land went to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. West of the Jordan, Joshua defeated kings from the hill country to the lowland. The list names each city’s king and counts “one” after each. It begins with Jericho and Ai. It includes Jerusalem, Hebron, Lachish, Hazor, and Megiddo. The total is thirty-one kings.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: Why does the list include victories on both sides of the Jordan? Who led each set of battles (verses 6–7)?

contextNote.title: A list gives conquest a remembered shape
contextNote.text: The chapter turns the battles of chapters 6–11 into a count. Each king gets the same short line and the word “one.” Verses 1–6 credit Moses with the eastern land. Verses 7–24 credit Joshua with the western land. Putting both together shows one work under two leaders. Each king is tied to one city, so the list is thirty-one towns. Chapter 13 then lists what was not yet taken.

passages.title: Remaining land and eastern inheritance
passages.summary: Joshua is old, and the LORD says much land remains to be taken. The Philistine regions, the Geshurites, and lands toward Lebanon are still unconquered. The LORD promises to drive those peoples out. Joshua must divide the western land among nine and a half tribes. The chapter then reviews the eastern land Moses gave. Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh each receive their towns there. Israel did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites. Levi receives no land, because the LORD is their inheritance.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: What duties remain after a tribe receives its share of land? What does the LORD say to Joshua in verse 1?

contextNote.title: A completed campaign is not complete possession
contextNote.text: Chapter 11:23 said Joshua took the whole land. Verse 1 now says “very much land” remains. Both statements stand in the book. The kings were beaten, but many places were not yet lived in. Verses 2–6 name the gaps, and verse 13 names peoples left in place. The LORD tells Joshua to divide the land anyway (verse 7). Each tribe receives a share that it must still go and settle.

passages.title: Caleb requests Hebron
passages.summary: Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads divide Canaan by lot. Caleb of Judah comes to Joshua at Gilgal. He recalls spying out the land at age forty and giving an honest report. Moses swore that the land he walked on would be his. Caleb is now eighty-five and says he is as strong as ever. He asks for the hill country where the Anakim live in walled cities. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. Then the land rests from war.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects Caleb’s faith with his request for an inheritance. What kind of land does Caleb ask for in verse 12?

contextNote.title: An earlier witness becomes a land claim
contextNote.text: Forty-five years earlier ten spies feared the Anakim’s walled cities (Numbers 13:28–33). Caleb said Israel could take the land. In verse 12 he asks for that same hill country, giants and all. He does not ask for an easy share as a reward. His words are careful: “It may be that the LORD will be with me.” His claim rests on Moses’s oath in verse 9. The man who trusted the promise then asks to act on it now.

passages.title: Judah’s land and Achsah’s request
passages.summary: Judah’s land is described by its borders, from the Salt Sea to the Great Sea. Caleb receives Hebron and drives out three sons of Anak. He offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Debir. Othniel takes the city and marries her. Achsah asks her father for springs of water to go with her dry land. Caleb gives her the upper and lower springs. Judah’s towns are then listed by region. Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The manual studies land distribution. Achsah’s land is in the dry South (verse 19). What does she ask her father to add?

contextNote.title: A land gift still needs water
contextNote.text: Achsah is given in marriage as a prize for a battle (verses 16–17). In verses 18–19 she acts for herself. She gets off her donkey and speaks to her father directly. Her land is in the South, and she needs water for it. A field there is of little use without a spring. She asks for “a blessing” and names it: springs of water. Caleb gives her two, the upper and the lower.

passages.title: Ephraim’s allotment
passages.summary: The lot for Joseph’s sons starts at the Jordan near Jericho. It runs through Bethel toward Beth Horon and ends at the sea. Manasseh and Ephraim take their inheritance. Ephraim’s border is traced from Ataroth to the brook of Kanah. Ephraim also has towns set inside Manasseh’s land. They did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer. Those Canaanites live among Ephraim and do forced labor.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: How does forced labor affect the Canaanites who remain? What two things does verse 10 say about Gezer?

contextNote.title: Settlement includes dependence within shared towns
contextNote.text: Most of the chapter is a border list. Verse 10 ends it with a failure and a result. Ephraim did not drive out the people of Gezer. The Canaanites stayed and became forced laborers. Israel once did forced labor in Egypt (Exodus 1:11). Now Israelites set that burden on others. The same note returns in 17:13 and in Judges 1:28–30.

passages.title: Manasseh and the daughters’ inheritance
passages.summary: Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, receives land on both sides of the Jordan. Zelophehad’s five daughters come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders. They say the LORD commanded Moses to give them an inheritance. They receive land among their father’s brothers. Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites and later forced them to work. Joseph’s people complain that one share is too small. Joshua tells them to clear the forest in the hill country. He says they can drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The manual studies the division of land. How do Zelophehad’s daughters state their claim in verse 4?

contextNote.title: A promised rule must reach actual families
contextNote.text: Numbers 27:7 gave these five women a promise years earlier. A promise on record still has to be carried out when land is handed over. In verse 4 they come to the same kind of court as before. They quote the command: the LORD told Moses to give them a share. The leaders do not argue. Verse 6 shows the effect on the count of Manasseh’s portions. The rule made in the wilderness now reaches an actual family.

passages.title: Shiloh and Benjamin’s portion
passages.summary: All Israel gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting. Seven tribes still have no land. Joshua asks how long they will put off taking it. Three men from each tribe walk the land and write it up in seven parts. Joshua casts lots for them before the LORD at Shiloh. The first lot is Benjamin’s, between Judah and Joseph. Its borders and towns are listed. Its towns include Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: What helps the tribes share the land? What does Joshua send the men to do in verse 8?

contextNote.title: An allotment requires shared knowledge of land
contextNote.text: Seven tribes are slow to move, and Joshua rebukes them (verse 3). His fix is practical. Men from each tribe must walk the land and describe it (verses 4, 8). Every tribe has its own surveyors, so no one divides it unseen. The written record comes back to Shiloh. There the shares are assigned by lot “before the LORD” (verse 10). People measure, and the lot decides who gets which part.

passages.title: Remaining allotments and Joshua’s town
passages.summary: Simeon’s share lies inside Judah’s, because Judah’s part was too large. Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali receive their borders and towns. Dan’s share is listed last. Dan’s people also go north and take the town of Leshem. When all the tribes have land, Israel gives Joshua a share. He asks for Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He builds up the town and lives there. The division is finished at Shiloh, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
passages.uncertainty: Markers show named places and approximate regions. They do not establish exact campaign roads, tribal boundaries, or the date of a conquest.

lds.text: The manual studies the division of land. When does Joshua receive his own land (verse 49)?

contextNote.title: The leader receives his portion last
contextNote.text: Chapters 14–19 hand out land tribe by tribe. Verse 49 says Joshua’s share comes when they “finished distributing.” The leader who ran the division takes his part last. He does not assign it to himself. The people give it, and verse 50 says it was by the LORD’s command. He asks for one town in his own tribe’s hills. Caleb opened the list of shares in chapter 14, and Joshua closes it.

passages.title: Cities of refuge
passages.summary: The LORD tells Joshua to set up the cities of refuge. A person who kills by accident may flee to one. He states his case to the elders at the city gate. They take him in and give him a place to live. They must not hand him over to the avenger of blood. He stays until he stands trial and until the high priest dies. Three cities are west of the Jordan: Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron. Three are east: Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan.

contextNote.title: Protection leaves room for a hearing
contextNote.text: Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19 ordered these cities. Here they are named and placed across the land. Verse 4 has the man explain himself at the gate before he enters. Verse 5 protects him because he “didn’t hate him before.” The test is intent, shown by the past between the two. Verse 6 still requires a trial before the community. Verse 9 opens the cities to foreigners as well as Israelites.

passages.title: Levitical towns and fulfillment
passages.summary: The Levite leaders come to Eleazar and Joshua at Shiloh. They recall that the LORD commanded towns and pasture for them. Each tribe gives towns from its own land. Aaron’s family receives thirteen towns in Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. The other Kohathites, the Gershonites, and the Merarites receive theirs by lot. In all the Levites receive forty-eight towns with pasture. The LORD gives Israel the land and rest on every side. Not one good promise of the LORD has failed.

contextNote.title: Sacred service depends on other households
contextNote.text: The Levites have no tribal territory (13:33). They must ask for what Moses promised them (verse 2). Verse 3 says the other tribes gave “out of their inheritance.” Every tribe loses some towns so the Levites can live. The towns are spread through all the tribes, not kept in one place. So those who serve at the sanctuary depend on every other household. Verse 45 then sums up the whole division: nothing the LORD promised failed.

passages.title: An altar and a dispute
passages.summary: Joshua thanks Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh and sends them home. Near the Jordan they build a large altar. The other tribes hear of it and gather at Shiloh for war. First they send Phinehas and ten leaders to ask what it means. They fear another sin like Peor or Achan’s. The eastern tribes say the altar is not for sacrifice. It is a witness that their children also belong to the LORD. Phinehas is satisfied, and the war is called off.

contextNote.title: A visible object can carry different meanings
contextNote.text: The western tribes see an altar and assume rebellion (verses 11–12). A second altar would break the rule of one place for sacrifice. They arm for war but send men to ask first. The builders give a meaning no one had guessed. They feared the Jordan would one day cut their children off (verses 24–25). The altar is a copy to look at, not a place to offer (verse 28). Asking before attacking prevents a war between brothers.

passages.title: Joshua’s farewell warning
passages.summary: Years later Joshua is old and calls Israel’s leaders together. He reminds them that the LORD fought for them. Nations still remain in the land, and the LORD will drive them out. Israel must keep the law of Moses and hold fast to the LORD. They must not serve the gods of those nations or marry among them. If they do, the LORD will stop driving the nations out. Those nations will become a snare, a whip, and thorns. As every good promise came true, so will the warnings.

contextNote.title: The farewell names limits to future security
contextNote.text: Joshua’s speech looks back at promises kept (verse 14). It also looks ahead with a condition. Verse 12 names the danger: clinging to the nations that remain. Verse 13 gives the result in four pictures: a snare, a trap, a scourge, thorns. The LORD’s help in war is not automatic. Verse 15 says the warnings are as sure as the blessings were. Judges 2:1–3 reports that this is what happened.

passages.title: The covenant at Shechem
passages.summary: Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem. He speaks for the LORD and retells the story from Abraham to the conquest. Their fathers served other gods beyond the River. The LORD brought them from Egypt and gave them land they did not work. Joshua tells them to choose whom they will serve. He says he and his house will serve the LORD. The people promise three times, and Joshua sets up a stone as a witness. Joshua dies at 110, and Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem.

contextNote.title: Land possession does not finish the story
contextNote.text: The people already live in the land, and the wars are over. Verse 15 treats the main question as still open: whom will you serve? Joshua names real rivals, the old family gods and the local ones. He gives his own answer first. When the people agree, he pushes back: “You can’t serve the LORD” (verse 19). Verse 23 shows why: foreign gods are still among them. The choice has to be made again by each generation (verse 31).

events.title: Joshua receives the charge
events.summary: After Moses dies, the LORD tells Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan. He promises to give them every place their feet tread. He says he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses. He tells Joshua three times to be strong and courageous. Joshua must keep the law and think on it day and night. Joshua tells the officers to prepare to cross in three days. He reminds Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh to fight beside their brothers. They promise to obey him as they obeyed Moses.
events.detail: Joshua is a new commander facing a war. The LORD’s orders in verses 6–9 say almost nothing about tactics. Three times he says to be strong and courageous. In between, verse 8 gives one practice: keep the law in his mouth always. Success is tied to doing “all that is written in it.” This matches the rule for kings in Deuteronomy 17:18–19. Israel’s leader does not stand above the law he enforces.

events.title: Rahab protects the spies
events.summary: Joshua secretly sends two spies to Jericho. They stay in the house of Rahab, a prostitute. The king sends for them, and Rahab hides them under flax on her roof. She tells the king’s men that the spies already left. She tells the spies the LORD has given Israel the land. She asks them to spare her family, and they swear to it. She lets them down by a cord from her window in the city wall. She must tie a scarlet cord there and keep her family inside.
events.detail: The spies were sent to learn about Jericho. What they learn comes from Rahab’s mouth. She retells the Red Sea and the defeat of two kings (verses 9–10). Verse 11 calls the LORD “God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.” Moses used nearly the same words in Deuteronomy 4:39. So the first clear statement of faith in the land comes from a Canaanite woman. She then acts on it at risk to herself (verses 4–6 and 15).

events.title: Crossing the Jordan
events.summary: Israel camps at the Jordan for three days. The officers tell the people to follow the ark at a distance. Joshua tells them to make themselves ready for the LORD’s wonders. The LORD says he will make Joshua great, as he was with Moses. The priests carry the ark to the river, which is in flood at harvest. When their feet touch the water, the river stops and piles up far upstream. The priests stand on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crosses over near Jericho.
events.detail: Verse 15 notes that the Jordan was in flood at harvest time. The river does not part while the people watch from the bank. Verse 13 ties the stopping to the priests’ feet resting in the water. They must step in while it is still running. Verse 17 has them stand in the riverbed until the whole nation is across. The priests go first and leave last. Verse 7 says the event also shows that God is with Joshua.

events.title: Stones for remembrance
events.summary: After the crossing, the LORD tells Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Each carries a stone from the riverbed where the priests stood. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan. About forty thousand armed men cross toward Jericho. That day the people honor Joshua as they had honored Moses. When the priests come out, the river returns and overflows its banks. Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there. The stones are for children who will ask what they mean.
events.detail: A pile of stones says nothing without someone to speak for it. Verse 6 expects children to ask what the stones mean. Verse 7 gives parents the answer to pass on. The stones come from the exact place the priests stood (verse 3). So they are evidence as well as a marker. Verses 21–24 repeat the question and link the Jordan to the Red Sea. The aim reaches past Israel: that all peoples may know the LORD’s hand.

events.title: Passover and the commander
events.summary: The kings of the land hear about the Jordan and lose heart. The LORD tells Joshua to circumcise the men born in the wilderness. The older generation had died there for not listening. The LORD says he has rolled away Egypt’s reproach, and the place is named Gilgal. Israel keeps the Passover in the plains of Jericho. They eat the produce of the land, and the manna stops. Near Jericho Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword. He is commander of the LORD’s army, and Joshua bows and removes his sandals.
events.detail: Joshua’s question in verse 13 offers two choices: for us or for our enemies. The man’s first word is “No.” He is not a soldier for either side to claim. He commands the LORD’s army, and Joshua is the one who must take a side. Joshua understands at once and falls on his face. He then asks the better question: what does his lord say? Verse 15 repeats what Moses heard at the bush (Exodus 3:5).

events.title: Jericho and Rahab’s rescue
events.summary: Jericho is shut tight. The LORD tells Joshua to march around it once a day for six days. Seven priests carry ram’s horn trumpets before the ark. On day seven they circle seven times and shout, and the wall falls flat. Israel destroys everyone in the city, young and old, and the animals. The two spies bring out Rahab and her whole family. The city is burned, and its metals go to the LORD’s treasury. Rahab lives in Israel from then on, and Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds Jericho.
events.detail: The chapter gives Jericho’s fall in verse 20 and its destruction in verse 21. Verse 21 lists who died: men, women, young, and old. Verses 22–25 then tell of one house that was spared. The spies keep the oath of 2:14 and bring out Rahab’s whole family. Verse 25 gives the reason: “she hid the messengers.” A Canaanite woman now lives “in the middle of Israel.” The account sets rescue beside destruction and does not explain away either.

events.title: Achan and defeat at Ai
events.summary: Achan of Judah secretly takes some of the goods devoted to the LORD. Israel sends about three thousand men against Ai, and they are driven back. Thirty-six die, and the people lose heart. Joshua falls before the ark and asks why God brought them over the Jordan. The LORD says Israel has sinned and stolen devoted things. The next morning Judah is singled out, then a family, then Achan. Achan confesses that he hid a robe, silver, and gold under his tent. Israel stones him and his household in the valley of Achor.
events.detail: Verse 1 blames “the children of Israel” for what one man did. Thirty-six soldiers die before anyone knows why (verse 5). Achan’s confession in verse 21 walks through the steps: saw, coveted, took. Then he hid the goods in the ground under his tent. What was buried in private had already cost lives in public. Verse 11 says the theft also involved deceit. The penalty falls on his household too, with no comment given (verses 24–25).

events.title: Ai and the law at Ebal
events.summary: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and to set an ambush behind Ai. Joshua hides men west of the city and camps the rest to the north. Israel pretends to flee, and every man of Ai chases them. Joshua stretches out his javelin, and the hidden men take and burn the city. Twelve thousand people of Ai die, and its king is hanged. Israel keeps the livestock and goods this time. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and writes the law on stones. He reads every word to all Israel, with the women, children, and foreigners.
events.detail: After two battles Joshua stops the war for a reading. Moses ordered this at Mount Ebal in Deuteronomy 27:2–8. Joshua builds the altar, writes the law on stones, and reads it all. Verse 34 says he read “the blessing and the curse.” Verse 35 names those who heard: women, little ones, and foreigners. None of these fought at Ai. The law belongs to the whole people, not only to its army.

events.title: The Gibeonite agreement
events.summary: The kings west of the Jordan join to fight Israel. The people of Gibeon choose a trick. They come with worn sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread, and claim a far country. Israel’s men taste their food and do not ask the LORD. Joshua makes a covenant to let them live, and the leaders swear to it. Three days later Israel learns that they live nearby. The people grumble, but the leaders will not break an oath sworn by the LORD. The Gibeonites become woodcutters and water carriers for the altar.
events.detail: Verse 14 names Israel’s mistake: they tested the bread and did not ask the LORD. The covenant in verse 15 rests on a lie the Gibeonites told. Three days later the truth comes out. The leaders still say, “We have sworn to them by the LORD” (verse 19). An oath in God’s name binds them even though they were tricked. So the Gibeonites live, as servants at the altar (verse 27). Their reason in verse 24 is the same fear Rahab named in 2:9–11.

events.title: The southern coalition
events.summary: Five Amorite kings, led by Jerusalem’s king, attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Gibeon begs Joshua not to abandon it. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and surprises them. The LORD throws them into confusion and sends great hailstones. Joshua asks for the sun and moon to stand still, and they do. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are later put to death. Joshua takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. He holds the southern land because the LORD fought for Israel.
events.detail: Gibeon won its treaty by a trick in chapter 9. Now the treaty brings an attack, and Gibeon calls for help (verse 6). Joshua could have let the kings remove a problem for him. He marches all night to keep the oath (verse 9). The LORD backs that choice with hail and a long day (verses 11–14). So this battle is fought for an ally Israel did not want. Second Samuel 21:1–2 later treats breaking this oath as a serious wrong.

events.title: Hazor and northern war
events.summary: Jabin king of Hazor gathers the northern kings with horses and chariots. Their army is like the sand of the seashore. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear. Joshua attacks suddenly at the waters of Merom and wins. He cripples their horses and burns their chariots, as the LORD said. He burns Hazor, the leading city, but not the other cities on their mounds. The war with these kings lasts a long time. Joshua takes the whole land, and the land rests from war.
events.detail: Chapters 10 and 11 can read like a quick sweep through the land. Verse 18 corrects that: “Joshua made war a long time.” Caleb’s words in 14:10 suggest several years had passed. Verse 13 adds that most cities were left standing, and only Hazor was burned. Verse 22 notes that some Anakim remained in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. So the summary “the whole land” in verse 23 has stated limits. Chapter 13:1 says much land still remained.

events.title: The defeated kings listed
events.summary: This chapter lists the kings Israel defeated. East of the Jordan, Moses defeated Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan. Their land went to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. West of the Jordan, Joshua defeated kings from the hill country to the lowland. The list names each city’s king and counts “one” after each. It begins with Jericho and Ai. It includes Jerusalem, Hebron, Lachish, Hazor, and Megiddo. The total is thirty-one kings.
events.detail: The chapter turns the battles of chapters 6–11 into a count. Each king gets the same short line and the word “one.” Verses 1–6 credit Moses with the eastern land. Verses 7–24 credit Joshua with the western land. Putting both together shows one work under two leaders. Each king is tied to one city, so the list is thirty-one towns. Chapter 13 then lists what was not yet taken.

events.title: Remaining land and eastern inheritance
events.summary: Joshua is old, and the LORD says much land remains to be taken. The Philistine regions, the Geshurites, and lands toward Lebanon are still unconquered. The LORD promises to drive those peoples out. Joshua must divide the western land among nine and a half tribes. The chapter then reviews the eastern land Moses gave. Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh each receive their towns there. Israel did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites. Levi receives no land, because the LORD is their inheritance.
events.detail: Chapter 11:23 said Joshua took the whole land. Verse 1 now says “very much land” remains. Both statements stand in the book. The kings were beaten, but many places were not yet lived in. Verses 2–6 name the gaps, and verse 13 names peoples left in place. The LORD tells Joshua to divide the land anyway (verse 7). Each tribe receives a share that it must still go and settle.

events.title: Caleb requests Hebron
events.summary: Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads divide Canaan by lot. Caleb of Judah comes to Joshua at Gilgal. He recalls spying out the land at age forty and giving an honest report. Moses swore that the land he walked on would be his. Caleb is now eighty-five and says he is as strong as ever. He asks for the hill country where the Anakim live in walled cities. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. Then the land rests from war.
events.detail: Forty-five years earlier ten spies feared the Anakim’s walled cities (Numbers 13:28–33). Caleb said Israel could take the land. In verse 12 he asks for that same hill country, giants and all. He does not ask for an easy share as a reward. His words are careful: “It may be that the LORD will be with me.” His claim rests on Moses’s oath in verse 9. The man who trusted the promise then asks to act on it now.

events.title: Judah’s land and Achsah’s request
events.summary: Judah’s land is described by its borders, from the Salt Sea to the Great Sea. Caleb receives Hebron and drives out three sons of Anak. He offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Debir. Othniel takes the city and marries her. Achsah asks her father for springs of water to go with her dry land. Caleb gives her the upper and lower springs. Judah’s towns are then listed by region. Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem.
events.detail: Achsah is given in marriage as a prize for a battle (verses 16–17). In verses 18–19 she acts for herself. She gets off her donkey and speaks to her father directly. Her land is in the South, and she needs water for it. A field there is of little use without a spring. She asks for “a blessing” and names it: springs of water. Caleb gives her two, the upper and the lower.

events.title: Ephraim’s allotment
events.summary: The lot for Joseph’s sons starts at the Jordan near Jericho. It runs through Bethel toward Beth Horon and ends at the sea. Manasseh and Ephraim take their inheritance. Ephraim’s border is traced from Ataroth to the brook of Kanah. Ephraim also has towns set inside Manasseh’s land. They did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer. Those Canaanites live among Ephraim and do forced labor.
events.detail: Most of the chapter is a border list. Verse 10 ends it with a failure and a result. Ephraim did not drive out the people of Gezer. The Canaanites stayed and became forced laborers. Israel once did forced labor in Egypt (Exodus 1:11). Now Israelites set that burden on others. The same note returns in 17:13 and in Judges 1:28–30.

events.title: Manasseh and the daughters’ inheritance
events.summary: Manasseh, Joseph’s firstborn, receives land on both sides of the Jordan. Zelophehad’s five daughters come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the leaders. They say the LORD commanded Moses to give them an inheritance. They receive land among their father’s brothers. Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites and later forced them to work. Joseph’s people complain that one share is too small. Joshua tells them to clear the forest in the hill country. He says they can drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots.
events.detail: Numbers 27:7 gave these five women a promise years earlier. A promise on record still has to be carried out when land is handed over. In verse 4 they come to the same kind of court as before. They quote the command: the LORD told Moses to give them a share. The leaders do not argue. Verse 6 shows the effect on the count of Manasseh’s portions. The rule made in the wilderness now reaches an actual family.

events.title: Shiloh and Benjamin’s portion
events.summary: All Israel gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting. Seven tribes still have no land. Joshua asks how long they will put off taking it. Three men from each tribe walk the land and write it up in seven parts. Joshua casts lots for them before the LORD at Shiloh. The first lot is Benjamin’s, between Judah and Joseph. Its borders and towns are listed. Its towns include Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem.
events.detail: Seven tribes are slow to move, and Joshua rebukes them (verse 3). His fix is practical. Men from each tribe must walk the land and describe it (verses 4, 8). Every tribe has its own surveyors, so no one divides it unseen. The written record comes back to Shiloh. There the shares are assigned by lot “before the LORD” (verse 10). People measure, and the lot decides who gets which part.

events.title: Remaining allotments and Joshua’s town
events.summary: Simeon’s share lies inside Judah’s, because Judah’s part was too large. Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali receive their borders and towns. Dan’s share is listed last. Dan’s people also go north and take the town of Leshem. When all the tribes have land, Israel gives Joshua a share. He asks for Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim. He builds up the town and lives there. The division is finished at Shiloh, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.

He does not assign it to himself. The people give it, and verse 50 says it was by the LORD’s command. He asks for one town in his own tribe’s hills. Caleb opened the list of shares in chapter 14, and Joshua closes it.

events.title: An altar and a dispute
events.summary: Joshua thanks Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh and sends them home. Near the Jordan they build a large altar. The other tribes hear of it and gather at Shiloh for war. First they send Phinehas and ten leaders to ask what it means. They fear another sin like Peor or Achan’s. The eastern tribes say the altar is not for sacrifice. It is a witness that their children also belong to the LORD. Phinehas is satisfied, and the war is called off.
events.detail: The western tribes see an altar and assume rebellion (verses 11–12). A second altar would break the rule of one place for sacrifice. They arm for war but send men to ask first. The builders give a meaning no one had guessed. They feared the Jordan would one day cut their children off (verses 24–25). The altar is a copy to look at, not a place to offer (verse 28). Asking before attacking prevents a war between brothers.

events.title: Joshua’s farewell warning
events.summary: Years later Joshua is old and calls Israel’s leaders together. He reminds them that the LORD fought for them. Nations still remain in the land, and the LORD will drive them out. Israel must keep the law of Moses and hold fast to the LORD. They must not serve the gods of those nations or marry among them. If they do, the LORD will stop driving the nations out. Those nations will become a snare, a whip, and thorns. As every good promise came true, so will the warnings.
events.detail: Joshua’s speech looks back at promises kept (verse 14). It also looks ahead with a condition. Verse 12 names the danger: clinging to the nations that remain. Verse 13 gives the result in four pictures: a snare, a trap, a scourge, thorns. The LORD’s help in war is not automatic. Verse 15 says the warnings are as sure as the blessings were. Judges 2:1–3 reports that this is what happened.

events.title: The covenant at Shechem
events.summary: Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem. He speaks for the LORD and retells the story from Abraham to the conquest. Their fathers served other gods beyond the River. The LORD brought them from Egypt and gave them land they did not work. Joshua tells them to choose whom they will serve. He says he and his house will serve the LORD. The people promise three times, and Joshua sets up a stone as a witness. Joshua dies at 110, and Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem.
events.detail: The people already live in the land, and the wars are over. Verse 15 treats the main question as still open: whom will you serve? Joshua names real rivals, the old family gods and the local ones. He gives his own answer first. When the people agree, he pushes back: “You can’t serve the LORD” (verse 19). Verse 23 shows why: foreign gods are still among them. The choice has to be made again by each generation (verse 31).

guides.title: Joshua: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The first witness comes from outside
steps.text: The spies were sent to learn about Jericho. What they learn comes from Rahab’s mouth. She retells the Red Sea and the defeat of two kings (verses 9–10). Verse 11 calls the LORD “God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.” Moses used nearly the same words in Deuteronomy 4:39. So the first clear statement of faith in the land comes from a Canaanite woman. She then acts on it at risk to herself (verses 4–6 and 15).

steps.title: An oath survives a failed decision
steps.text: Verse 14 names Israel’s mistake: they tested the bread and did not ask the LORD. The covenant in verse 15 rests on a lie the Gibeonites told. Three days later the truth comes out. The leaders still say, “We have sworn to them by the LORD” (verse 19). An oath in God’s name binds them even though they were tricked. So the Gibeonites live, as servants at the altar (verse 27). Their reason in verse 24 is the same fear Rahab named in 2:9–11.

steps.title: Land possession does not finish the story
steps.text: The people already live in the land, and the wars are over. Verse 15 treats the main question as still open: whom will you serve? Joshua names real rivals, the old family gods and the local ones. He gives his own answer first. When the people agree, he pushes back: “You can’t serve the LORD” (verse 19). Verse 23 shows why: foreign gods are still among them. The choice has to be made again by each generation (verse 31).

chapterMaps.narrative: After Moses dies, the LORD tells Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan. He promises to give them every place their feet tread. He says he will be with Joshua as he was with Moses. He tells Joshua three times to be strong and courageous. Joshua must keep the law and think on it day and night. Joshua tells the officers to prepare to cross in three days. He reminds Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh to fight beside their brothers. They promise to obey him as they obeyed Moses.

chapterMaps.narrative: Joshua secretly sends two spies to Jericho. They stay in the house of Rahab, a prostitute. The king sends for them, and Rahab hides them under flax on her roof. She tells the king’s men that the spies already left. She tells the spies the LORD has given Israel the land. She asks them to spare her family, and they swear to it. She lets them down by a cord from her window in the city wall. She must tie a scarlet cord there and keep her family inside.

chapterMaps.narrative: Israel camps at the Jordan for three days. The officers tell the people to follow the ark at a distance. Joshua tells them to make themselves ready for the LORD’s wonders. The LORD says he will make Joshua great, as he was with Moses. The priests carry the ark to the river, which is in flood at harvest. When their feet touch the water, the river stops and piles up far upstream. The priests stand on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crosses over near Jericho.

chapterMaps.narrative: After the crossing, the LORD tells Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Each carries a stone from the riverbed where the priests stood. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan. About forty thousand armed men cross toward Jericho. That day the people honor Joshua as they had honored Moses. When the priests come out, the river returns and overflows its banks. Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there. The stones are for children who will ask what they mean.

The older generation had died there for not listening. The LORD says he has rolled away Egypt’s reproach, and the place is named Gilgal. Israel keeps the Passover in the plains of Jericho. They eat the produce of the land, and the manna stops. Near Jericho Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword. He is commander of the LORD’s army, and Joshua bows and removes his sandals.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jericho is shut tight. The LORD tells Joshua to march around it once a day for six days. Seven priests carry ram’s horn trumpets before the ark. On day seven they circle seven times and shout, and the wall falls flat. Israel destroys everyone in the city, young and old, and the animals. The two spies bring out Rahab and her whole family. The city is burned, and its metals go to the LORD’s treasury. Rahab lives in Israel from then on, and Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds Jericho.

chapterMaps.narrative: Achan of Judah secretly takes some of the goods devoted to the LORD. Israel sends about three thousand men against Ai, and they are driven back. Thirty-six die, and the people lose heart. Joshua falls before the ark and asks why God brought them over the Jordan. The LORD says Israel has sinned and stolen devoted things. The next morning Judah is singled out, then a family, then Achan. Achan confesses that he hid a robe, silver, and gold under his tent. Israel stones him and his household in the valley of Achor.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and to set an ambush behind Ai. Joshua hides men west of the city and camps the rest to the north. Israel pretends to flee, and every man of Ai chases them. Joshua stretches out his javelin, and the hidden men take and burn the city. Twelve thousand people of Ai die, and its king is hanged. Israel keeps the livestock and goods this time. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and writes the law on stones. He reads every word to all Israel, with the women, children, and foreigners.

chapterMaps.narrative: The kings west of the Jordan join to fight Israel. The people of Gibeon choose a trick. They come with worn sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread, and claim a far country. Israel’s men taste their food and do not ask the LORD. Joshua makes a covenant to let them live, and the leaders swear to it. Three days later Israel learns that they live nearby. The people grumble, but the leaders will not break an oath sworn by the LORD. The Gibeonites become woodcutters and water carriers for the altar.

chapterMaps.narrative: Five Amorite kings, led by Jerusalem’s king, attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Gibeon begs Joshua not to abandon it. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and surprises them. The LORD throws them into confusion and sends great hailstones. Joshua asks for the sun and moon to stand still, and they do. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are later put to death. Joshua takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. He holds the southern land because the LORD fought for Israel.

textRoutes.title: Crossing the Jordan
textRoutes.summary: Israel camps at the Jordan for three days. The officers tell the people to follow the ark at a distance. Joshua tells them to make themselves ready for the LORD’s wonders. The LORD says he will make Joshua great, as he was with Moses. The priests carry the ark to the river, which is in flood at harvest. When their feet touch the water, the river stops and piles up far upstream. The priests stand on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan. All Israel crosses over near Jericho.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 15 notes that the Jordan was in flood at harvest time. The river does not part while the people watch from the bank. Verse 13 ties the stopping to the priests’ feet resting in the water. They must step in while it is still running. Verse 17 has them stand in the riverbed until the whole nation is across. The priests go first and leave last. Verse 7 says the event also shows that God is with Joshua.

textRoutes.title: Stones for remembrance
textRoutes.summary: After the crossing, the LORD tells Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe. Each carries a stone from the riverbed where the priests stood. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan. About forty thousand armed men cross toward Jericho. That day the people honor Joshua as they had honored Moses. When the priests come out, the river returns and overflows its banks. Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the twelve stones there. The stones are for children who will ask what they mean.
textRoutes.detail: A pile of stones says nothing without someone to speak for it. Verse 6 expects children to ask what the stones mean. Verse 7 gives parents the answer to pass on. The stones come from the exact place the priests stood (verse 3). So they are evidence as well as a marker. Verses 21–24 repeat the question and link the Jordan to the Red Sea. The aim reaches past Israel: that all peoples may know the LORD’s hand.

textRoutes.title: The southern coalition
textRoutes.summary: Five Amorite kings, led by Jerusalem’s king, attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Gibeon begs Joshua not to abandon it. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal and surprises them. The LORD throws them into confusion and sends great hailstones. Joshua asks for the sun and moon to stand still, and they do. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah and are later put to death. Joshua takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. He holds the southern land because the LORD fought for Israel.
textRoutes.detail: Gibeon won its treaty by a trick in chapter 9. Now the treaty brings an attack, and Gibeon calls for help (verse 6). Joshua could have let the kings remove a problem for him. He marches all night to keep the oath (verse 9). The LORD backs that choice with hail and a long day (verses 11–14). So this battle is fought for an ally Israel did not want. Second Samuel 21:1–2 later treats breaking this oath as a serious wrong.

textRoutes.title: An altar and a dispute
textRoutes.summary: Joshua thanks Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh and sends them home. Near the Jordan they build a large altar. The other tribes hear of it and gather at Shiloh for war. First they send Phinehas and ten leaders to ask what it means. They fear another sin like Peor or Achan’s. The eastern tribes say the altar is not for sacrifice. It is a witness that their children also belong to the LORD. Phinehas is satisfied, and the war is called off.
textRoutes.detail: The western tribes see an altar and assume rebellion (verses 11–12). A second altar would break the rule of one place for sacrifice. They arm for war but send men to ask first. The builders give a meaning no one had guessed. They feared the Jordan would one day cut their children off (verses 24–25). The altar is a copy to look at, not a place to offer (verse 28). Asking before attacking prevents a war between brothers.
